porbos.title: The Alliance of Hawazin • On the Road to Hunayn • Dawn in the Valley • They Returned at a Single Call • The Witness for the Salab • The Uncle and Nephew of Awtas • Beneath the Fortress of Ta’if

blocks.1: Makkah fell so fast that before any tribe of Arabia could make sense of anything, it was all over. Those who accepted it with closed mouths bowed their heads in silence. But the necks of the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes were stiff. To sit quietly on this happy day of the Muslims offended their self-respect. They gathered around Malik ibn ‘Awf al-Nasri. The decision was made: fight the Muslims. He set out with the soldiers, taking along their wealth, women and children too. The thinking was: the one who has left family and goods behind him, where will he flee to? They came and pitched camp at Awtas. There was an old man there, Duraid ibn al-Simmah. Once a famous warrior; now he could not see, but his mind was still sharp. He asked, where are we? The people said, at Awtas. He said, a good place, just right for horses; neither hard nor soft. But from where is there coming to my ears the cry of camels, the braying of donkeys, the bleating of sheep and the weeping of children? Malik said, I have placed behind every soldier his family and property, so that they fight to protect them. Duraid said, lamb! Does anyone stop the defeated from fleeing? If you win, soldiers with arrows and swords will be of use; if you lose, you will be disgraced along with women, children and property. Malik replied, by Allah, I will not do that. You have grown old, and your intellect too is blunt. Either Hawazin will obey me, or I will put this sword into my belly and bring it out through my back. Duraid fell silent. He only said,
blocks.3: Alas, if only I were young today! Then I would run off at a trot. I would lead the horses with long hair and of middling kind.{{1}}
blocks.4: The old man could not see, but he had sensed the outcome. To the commander who counts his own stubbornness greater than listening, who explains the old man’s reckoning to him? Stubbornness sometimes turns all one’s own wealth against oneself. We do the same. The advice that is disliked we throw away as old; later we pay its price.
blocks.6: In the month of Shawwal, after nineteen days in Makkah, the Prophet {{1}} set out toward Hunayn. With him the ten thousand of Madinah, and a large band of the new Muslims of Makkah. He left ‘Attab ibn Usayd in charge of Makkah. He borrowed a hundred coats of mail from Safwan ibn Umayyah. A rider rushed in and brought news: I have seen from the top of such-and-such mountain, Hawazin, with their wealth, camels and goats, the whole tribe, have gathered at Hunayn. The Prophet {{2}} smiled and said, in sha’ Allah, tomorrow all this will be spoils for the Muslims.{{3}}
blocks.8: On the way there was a huge green jujube tree. Its name was Dhat Anwat. In the Jahili era the Arabs used to hang their weapons on that tree, slaughter animals beneath it, hold fairs. A few new people in the Muslim army said, O Messenger of Allah, as they have a Dhat Anwat, make one for us too. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.10: This is exactly what the people of Musa said, ‘Make for us a god too, as they have gods.’ By the One in whose hand is my soul, you will surely follow the ways of those before you.{{1}}
blocks.11: People who had only just left shirk. The marks of the old pictures still in their eyes. This mistake they made out of mere ignorance; the Prophet {{1}} corrected it at once. Seeing big trees, big shrines, big names, in us too the same desire stirs: let us make something for ourselves too, holding which we will get blessing. So the struggle of tawhid is not only against idols, but against the old mould of idols. Seeing the vast gathering of the army, from some people’s mouths it slipped out, today we are so many; today we will not lose. The word reached the Prophet’s {{2}} ears. He was deeply hurt.{{3}}
blocks.12: At Badr Allah helped three hundred and thirteen. Today twelve thousand. The help has not changed; what has changed is the address of reliance. The strength that relies on its own numbers, knowledge, rank, money, before it Allah sends a small test, so that it may remember who is the owner of everything.
blocks.14: That night Hawazin reached first. Malik ibn ‘Awf placed archers, two or four at a time, behind every cleft and cave of the valley of Hunayn. The order was, as soon as the Muslim army is seen, shoot arrows all together; then everyone will pounce. In the dim light of dawn the Prophet {{1}} drew up the army and distributed the banners. The army descended into the narrow valley. It did not occur to anyone that there could be people behind every rock. Suddenly a rain of arrows from all sides. Then the enemy pounced.{{2}}
blocks.15: Scattered. No one had time to look at anyone. Some men of Makkah, who had not yet brought Islam, shouted, today their magic has been caught. But who was on the field? Someone later asked Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA), did you flee on the day of Hunayn? He said,
blocks.17: I bear witness, the Prophet {{1}} did not retreat. The people who had rushed ahead in haste were the ones scattered; Hawazin showered arrows on them. And Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith was holding the head of his white mule, and the Prophet {{2}} was saying, I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the descendant of ‘Abd al-Muttalib.{{3}}
blocks.19: A man on a white mule, facing the enemy. His cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith holding the mule’s head, his uncle ‘Abbas pulling the stirrup. Everyone is telling him to turn back, to stop; he goes forward, singing, I am the Prophet, no lie. One who is on the truth can, in the face of fear, say his identity in an even louder voice. Even if a single man stands in a crowd of fleeing people, there the honour of the whole caravan is kept alive. The Qur’an has told of that day in this way,
blocks.21: In fact Allah has helped you in many places, and (especially) on the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers had made you proud. But that large number was of no use to you, and the earth, despite its vastness, became narrow for you. Then you turned your backs and fled from the battlefield.{{1}}
blocks.22: They Returned at a Single Call
blocks.23: The Prophet {{1}} said to his uncle ‘Abbas, call. ‘Abbas (RA) was a man of a very loud voice. As loudly as he could, he called,
blocks.25: Hey, Ashab al-Samurah, where are you?{{1}}
blocks.28: By Allah, on hearing my call they came back the way a cow returns on hearing the call of her calf. They began to say, labbayk, labbayk!{{1}}
blocks.30: Some could not turn their camels. They took off their iron mail, threw it over their necks, shield and sword in hand, let the camel go, and themselves ran toward the call. As soon as a hundred gathered, fighting again. The call went to the Ansar: Ya ma‘shar al-Ansar! The call to the Ansar narrowed further and finally came to rest on one branch of the Khazraj. The Prophet {{1}}, rising up on the mule’s back, looked toward the fighting and said,
blocks.32: Now the battlefield has heated up.{{1}}
blocks.33: Then he took a few pebbles in his hand and threw them toward the faces of the disbelievers. He said, by the Lord of Muhammad, they are defeated. Within a little while the situation reversed. The enemy who that morning had scattered the Muslims were now fleeing. Seventy leaders of the enemy side were killed. Six thousand prisoners, herds of camels and goats, four thousand uqiyyah of silver came into the Muslims’ hands. The Qur’an has told of that moment in this way,
blocks.35: Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and the believers, and sent down troops which you did not see. And He punished those who had disbelieved. And this is the recompense of the disbelievers.{{1}}
blocks.36: Allah sent an army that could not be seen with the eye. The one who relies on his own strength, his test comes through strength itself. The one who returns at a single call, for him help comes down from the sky. For returning, no day is too late. When we make a mistake we think, there is no road back. Those who returned at ‘Abbas’s one call, all of them had been fleeing only a moment before.
blocks.38: After the battle the Prophet {{1}} sat and announced,
blocks.40: Whoever has killed someone, and has proof for it, his is the salab.{{1}}
blocks.41: Abu Qatadah (RA) had seen that day a polytheist pressing hard on a Muslim. He had gone around from behind and struck that polytheist on the neck with his sword. He embraced him so tightly that he smelled death. Then the man died, he was freed. Hearing the Prophet’s {{1}} announcement Abu Qatadah stood up and said, who will bear witness for me? Then he sat down. The Prophet {{2}} said it again. He stood up again. Three times. The third time one man stood up and said, O Messenger of Allah, he has spoken the truth. His salab is with me. Please satisfy him on my behalf. Then Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) said, by Allah, that will not be. Leaving out one of Allah’s lions, who fights for Allah and His Messenger, will you be given his salab? The Prophet {{3}} said, he has spoken rightly. He gave the salab to Abu Qatadah. Abu Qatadah sold that mail and bought a date orchard. His first wealth in Islam. Claim, proof, witness. Even amid the excitement of the day of Hunayn these three steps were not skipped. When someone wanted to get a member of his own household something in place of bravery, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq stopped it, and the Messenger {{4}} called him right. For one who sits in the place of distributing, his task is to remember who is the rightful one; not who is sitting in front.
blocks.42: The Uncle and Nephew of Awtas
blocks.43: The fugitives split in three directions: some to Ta’if, some to Nakhlah, some to Awtas. The Prophet {{1}} sent an army toward Awtas with Abu ‘Amir (RA) as commander. With him his nephew Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari. There old Duraid ibn al-Simmah was killed. But an arrow shot by a Jushami polytheist went and pierced Abu ‘Amir’s knee. Abu Musa rushed up and asked, uncle, who struck you? Abu ‘Amir pointed, that is the man who shot me with the arrow. Abu Musa ran after him. The man began to flee. Abu Musa shouted, are you not ashamed? Stop! The man stopped. Two sword blows each passed between the two. Abu Musa killed him. Returning he said, uncle, Allah has killed your companion. Abu ‘Amir said, pull this arrow out. As it came out, water spurted from there. Abu ‘Amir said, nephew, give my salam to the Prophet {{2}}, and say, let him seek forgiveness for me. Abu ‘Amir made Abu Musa commander before he went. A little later he died. Abu Musa came back and went to the Prophet {{3}}. The Prophet {{4}} was then lying on a bed woven of palm-fibre rope; the marks of the bed had sunk into his back and ribs. Abu Musa gave all the news, and Abu ‘Amir’s salam. The Prophet {{5}} asked for water and made wudu’. He raised both hands. Abu Musa says, I saw the whiteness of his armpits. He said,
blocks.45: O Allah, forgive ‘Ubayd Abu ‘Amir. O Allah, on the Day of Resurrection place him above many of Your creation.{{1}}
blocks.47: Abu Musa then said, O Messenger of Allah, for me too. The Prophet {{1}} said, O Allah, forgive the sins of ‘Abdullah ibn Qays, and on the Day of Resurrection admit him to a place of honour. The last words of a commander on the battlefield were, tell the Prophet {{2}} to seek forgiveness for me. At the edge of death no one spoke of wealth, house, children. Only a du‘a. And the one from whom that du‘a was asked, leaving his busyness aside, made wudu’, raised his hands. When we hear news of someone’s illness we say, please make du‘a. How many of us raise our hands right then?
blocks.49: The greater part of the fugitives had gone and entered the fortress of Ta’if, with the commander Malik ibn ‘Awf. Having collected the spoils, the Prophet {{1}} went on the road to Ta’if. Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA) went ahead with a thousand soldiers. On the way Malik had a fort at a place called Liyyah. That was razed to the ground. Then the camp near the fortress of Ta’if. From inside the fortress arrows and heated iron spikes began to come down. Twelve Muslims were martyred, many were wounded. The camp had to be moved far away, to where today’s Ta’if mosque stands. The Prophet {{2}} set up a catapult, an attempt was made to breach the fortress walls. An attempt to enter under a wooden cover and burn the wall was also made, but it failed against the heated iron blades. After this the Prophet {{3}} said to cut down the grape orchards, to put the enemy under pressure. The Companions began to cut. Thaqif then, invoking Allah and kinship, asked to stop cutting the trees. The Prophet {{4}}, looking to Allah and kinship, stopped the cutting. It was announced, whoever leaves the fortress and comes to us is free. Twenty-three came out; one of them came down the wall hanging from a pulley, so he was named Abu Bakrah. The Prophet {{5}} freed them all.{{6}}
blocks.50: Days dragged on. The fortress did not budge. The Prophet {{1}} consulted Nawfal ibn Mu‘awiyah. He said, they are like a fox hiding in a hole; if you press hard you can catch it, if you leave it will not harm you. The Prophet {{2}} firmed up the intention to return.{{3}}
blocks.51: The moment it was said to the Companions it felt heavy. Return without victory? The Prophet {{1}} did not give a counter-argument to any argument. He only said, very well, go to the fighting tomorrow morning. They went. The result was wounds, blood, wounded companions. In the evening the Prophet {{2}} said again,
blocks.53: We are, in sha’ Allah, returning tomorrow.{{1}}
blocks.54: Now their hearts were cooled. Gladly they accepted, began to prepare for the return. Seeing this scene the Prophet {{1}} smiled. On the way back he taught the Companions a du‘a,
blocks.56: Say, we are returning, repenting, worshipping, praising our Lord.{{1}}
blocks.57: Someone said, O Messenger of Allah, make a curse upon Thaqif. He made du‘a, O Allah, guide Thaqif, bring them back.{{1}}
blocks.58: The nation that was shooting arrows from the top of the fortress, shedding the Muslims’ blood — for it, what came to his lips was not a curse, but a prayer of guidance. And Allah had heard that prayer. The next year Thaqif themselves sent a delegation to Madinah. That story is in Dars 24. When we are struck by someone we curse; at words flung from the top of a fortress we get angry. And he was struck with arrows. Struck, he prayed for guidance. There is another lesson too. The leader does not always impose his own decision. Where people want to learn by first stumbling, he sometimes lets them stumble; then the right decision comes with a cool head. For the one whose decision it is, the duty is not only to announce it; it is also to know when the door of the listener’s heart will open.

footnotes.0: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 677–678 (Ibn Ishaq’s narration; Fath al-Bari 8/27, 42). Duraid ibn al-Simmah, the aged war-expert of Banu Jusham, still a disbeliever then; Malik ibn ‘Awf al-Nasri, the commander of Hawazin. A free rendering of the poem. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.1: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 679 (borrowing a hundred iron coats of mail with equipment from Safwan ibn Umayyah; appointing ‘Attab ibn Usayd in charge in Makkah; sending Abu Hadrad al-Aslami as a spy to the enemy camp). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.2: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 679 (the horseman’s news; the Prophet’s {{1}} smile and ‘in sha’ Allah tomorrow this will be spoils for the Muslims’; the guard of Anas ibn Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi; the incident of Dhat Anwat). The ten thousand of the Madinah army and two thousand new Makkan Muslims, twelve thousand in all (al-Rahiq); in note 19 of Tawdih al-Qur’an the number of Muslim soldiers is fourteen thousand, in Bukhari 4333 Anas (RA): ‘ten thousand and the tulaqa’’. No number is set in the dars, because the sources do not agree. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.3: Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 2180 (from Abu Waqid al-Laythi (RA)); al-Tirmidhi: hasan sahih. Musnad Ahmad 21897 (Arna’ut: the chain is sahih, on the condition of the two Shaykhs); al-Albani (Jilbab al-Mar’ah 202): sahih. In one version of al-Tirmidhi the incident is said to be ‘on the road to Khaybar’; in Ahmad’s narration ‘on the road to Hunayn’, and al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (pp. 679–680) also says so; so here it is the road to Hunayn. ‘Dhat Anwat’ is a jujube tree. The verse is Surah al-A‘raf 7:138.
footnotes.4: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Tawbah 9:25, p. 530, note 19 (reading the printed page): ‘The Muslims had always won against greater armies despite their own small numbers. This time, since their numbers too were vast, from some of their mouths it slipped out that today our numbers are very many. So today we cannot be defeated by anyone at all. That the Muslims would rely on their own numbers instead of Allah the Exalted, this did not please Allah the Exalted.’ Al-Rahiq, p. 680: the Prophet {{1}} was deeply hurt by this remark.
footnotes.5: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 680 (at night Malik ibn ‘Awf’s placing of soldiers in the valley of Hunayn; at dawn the Prophet’s {{1}} arranging the army, distributing banners; the sudden rain of arrows; the separation of the vanguard of Banu Sulaym; the remark of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb (RA) and the words of Kaladah ibn Hanbal). In Bukhari 4315 Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA): ‘the hasty people went ahead, Hawazin showered them with arrows.’ Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari 4315 (from Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA); via Abu Ishaq). On the same subject Ahmad 18468 (Arna’ut: the chain is sahih), Ibn Hibban 4770 (Arna’ut: sahih). The rajaz: ‘ana al-nabiyyu la kadhib, ana ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib’. The statement is not a poem; it came out of the mouth as rhythm.
footnotes.7: Disagreement on the number: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum, p. 681 (by Ibn Ishaq’s view nine; by Imam al-Nawawi’s view twelve; Musnad Ahmad 1/453–454 and al-Hakim 2/117, Ibn Mas‘ud (RA): eighty Muhajirun and Ansar; Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 1689, Ibn ‘Umar (RA): there were not even a hundred with him). The chain of the narration of eighty in Ahmad 4336 Arna’ut called weak, Ahmad Shakir called sahih; so no fixed number has been set in the dars.
footnotes.8: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Tawbah 9:25, p. 530 (matched word for word by reading the printed page); note 19: a summary of the incident of Hunayn, the number of Muslim soldiers, the gathering of Banu Hawazin under Malik ibn ‘Awf, the archers’ sudden attack and ‘Abbas (RA)’s call.
footnotes.9: Sahih Muslim 1775 (from ‘Abbas ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib (RA), via Kathir ibn al-‘Abbas; sahih): ‘That day I and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith did not leave the Prophet’s {{1}} side; when the Muslims drew back the Prophet {{2}} urged his white mule toward the disbelievers; I was holding the mule’s rein and stopping it; the Prophet {{3}} said, ‘Abbas, call Ashab al-Samurah’; ‘Abbas (RA) was a man of a very loud voice. ‘Samurah’ is the acacia tree of the Pledge of al-Ridwan; Ashab al-Samurah means the Companions of that pledge.
footnotes.10: Sahih Muslim 1775. In Sahih al-Bukhari 4333, Anas (RA): when the Prophet {{1}} said ‘ya ma‘shar al-Ansar’ they said, ‘labbayka ya Rasul Allah wa sa‘dayk, nahnu bayna yadayk’. By number the call to the Ansar was later narrowed down to ‘Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj’ (Muslim 1775).
footnotes.11: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 682 (‘Abbas (RA)’s call ‘O people of the acacia!’; whoever’s camel would not turn on the return would take off his iron mail, throw it over his neck, leave the mount and run toward the call with shield and sword; the attack as soon as a hundred gathered; the call at one point confined to Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj; the Prophet {{1}} threw a handful of earth and said ‘shahat al-wujuh’). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.12: Sahih Muslim 1775: ‘hadha hina hamiya al-watis’; later the Prophet {{1}} took a few pebbles and threw them toward the faces of the disbelievers, saying, ‘inhazamu wa rabbi Muhammad’, that is, by the Lord of Muhammad, they are defeated. ‘Watis’ is an oven or hearth; a proverb for the war reaching its peak. From Anas (RA), Bukhari 4333: the Prophet {{2}} dismounted from his mount and said, ‘ana ‘abdullahi wa rasuluhu’.
footnotes.13: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Tawbah 9:26, p. 531 (matched word for word by reading the printed page); note 20: ‘in the hearts of the Muslims who returned on hearing ‘Abbas (RA)’s call Allah created such relief that the terror from the enemy side vanished.’ Note 19: seventy leaders of Banu Hawazin killed, Malik ibn ‘Awf left his family and wealth and took refuge in the fortress of Ta’if; six thousand prisoners; vast livestock and four thousand uqiyyah of silver as spoils.
footnotes.14: Sahih al-Bukhari 3142 (from Abu Qatadah (RA); sahih), Sunan Abi Dawud 2717 (al-Albani: sahih); Sahih Muslim 1751 also has the same incident. ‘Salab’: the weapons, armour and clothes found on a slain enemy. ‘La halla-hi idhan’: by Allah, never; ‘usd Allah’: Allah’s lion. This ruling of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) was endorsed by the Prophet {{1}}. ‘Makhraf’: a date orchard; Abu Qatadah (RA) sold the mail and bought an orchard among Banu Salimah.
footnotes.15: Sahih al-Bukhari 4323, 2884, 6383; Sahih Muslim 2498 (from Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari (RA); sahih): the Prophet {{1}} asked for water and made wudu’, raised both hands (Abu Musa says, I saw the whiteness of his armpits), then this du‘a. When Abu Musa asked for du‘a for himself he said, ‘O Allah, forgive the sins of ‘Abdullah ibn Qays and on the Day of Resurrection admit him to a place of honour.’ Bukhari and Muslim, both agreed upon.
footnotes.16: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 683 (the fleeing enemy splitting in three directions: one group to Ta’if, one to Nakhlah, one to Awtas; Abu ‘Amir al-Ash‘ari (RA) was the commander of the army sent toward Awtas, he was martyred there; the horsemen pursuing toward Nakhlah caught Duraid ibn al-Simmah and had him killed by Rabi‘ah ibn Rufay‘ (RA)). In Bukhari 4323 Abu Musa (RA): ‘Duraid was killed’. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.17: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 683–687 (the Ghazwah of Ta’if is the last part of Hunayn itself; the vanguard of a thousand soldiers of Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA); the razing of Malik ibn ‘Awf’s fort at Liyyah; the use of the manjaniq and a wooden ‘tank’ (dabbabah) toward the fortress wall, several martyred by thrown heated iron spikes; the martyrdom of twelve Muslims; stopping when Thaqif, on the cutting of the grape orchards, invoked Allah and kinship; twenty-three coming out on the announcement ‘whoever comes out of the fortress is free’, Abu Bakrah (RA) came down hanging on a pulley, hence the name ‘Abu Bakrah’). Disagreement on the time of the siege: forty days in the narration of Imam Muslim from Anas (RA) (al-Rahiq mentions); in others’ view twenty, eighteen, fifteen days; Fath al-Bari 8/45. On the chain of Abu Bakrah (RA)’s narration (al-Bazzar 9/132, Majma‘ al-Zawa’id 6/193) there is an objection of weakness because of Abu al-Minhal al-Bakrawi. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence. ‘The mosque of Ta’if’: al-Rahiq, p. 685: where the Companions moved the camp and returned to, a mosque was built there later.
footnotes.18: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 686 (the counsel of Nawfal ibn Mu‘awiyah al-Dili: ‘they are like a fox hiding in a hole; if you press hard you can catch it, if you leave it will not harm you’). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.19: Sahih al-Bukhari 4325 (from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (RA); sahih); Sahih Ibn Hibban 4779 (Arna’ut: the chain is sahih, on the condition of the two Shaykhs). The full narration: ‘The Prophet {{1}} besieged Ta’if, did not get anything from them. He said, in sha’ Allah we are returning. That felt heavy to the Companions; they said, return without conquest? The Prophet {{2}} said, go to the fighting in the morning. They went, were wounded. Then he said, we are returning tomorrow in sha’ Allah. That pleased them; the Prophet {{3}} laughed (Sufyan: smiled).’ In al-Rahiq (p. 686) this is told as the announcement incident of ‘Umar (RA); in the Bukhari text who made the announcement is not given.
footnotes.20: The original text of this du‘a on returning: Sahih al-Bukhari 3084 (‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (RA): the Prophet {{1}}, returning from a journey, would say takbir three times and say, ‘a’ibuna in sha’ Allahu ta’ibuna ‘abiduna hamiduna li-rabbina sajidun; sadaqa Allahu wa‘dahu wa nasara ‘abdahu wa hazama al-ahzaba wahdahu’); Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 3440 (al-Tirmidhi: hasan sahih; al-Albani: sahih). Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum, p. 687: on returning from Ta’if he told the Companions to recite this du‘a (Sirah-based part).
footnotes.21: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 687 (when some asked the Prophet {{1}} to curse Thaqif he said, ‘O Allah, guide Thaqif, bring them back’); this narration is in Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 3942 (al-Tirmidhi: hasan sahih gharib), but al-Albani in Da‘if al-Tirmidhi 3942 and Difa‘ ‘an al-Hadith 34 called it weak; because of Abu al-Zubayr’s ‘an‘anah, weakness of the chain in ‘Hidayat al-Ruwat 5941’. The sense of the incident agrees with other sahih narrations (Sahih al-Bukhari 3231, the first journey to Ta’if; Dars 9 of this series of dars). In this dars it has come only as a scene.

quiz.q: Who was the commander of Hawazin at Hunayn?
Who rebuked Malik with ‘lamb!’ for his decision to bring family and property along at Awtas?
quiz.e: None can stop the defeated from fleeing, he said.

quiz.q: What was ‘Dhat Anwat’?
o: The acacia of the Pledge of al-Ridwan
The gate of the fortress of Ta’if

quiz.q: On setting out for Hunayn, whom did the Prophet ﷺ leave in charge of Makkah?
quiz.e: The mail was borrowed from Safwan.

quiz.q: How many coats of mail did the Prophet ﷺ borrow from Safwan ibn Umayyah?
In the incident of Dhat Anwat, to what did the Prophet ﷺ liken the new Muslims’ request?
o: The demand of the people of Musa

quiz.q: What is learned from the statement ‘today we are so many, today we will not lose’?
o: Help comes by reliance on Allah
It is improper to fight without a big army
Taking new Muslims along was a mistake
Learning about the enemy is unnecessary

quiz.q: A new Muslim friend says ‘let us make something for ourselves too, holding which we will get blessing’; which incident does this match?
In which incident is the result of excessive reliance on one’s own numbers, knowledge or money seen?

porbos.title: The Tent at Ji‘ranah • The Weeping of the Ansar • The Delegates of Hawazin • A Complaint in the Name of Justice

blocks.1: Returning from Ta’if, the Prophet {{1}} halted at Ji‘ranah, where the spoils of Hunayn had been kept. Six thousand prisoners, twenty-four thousand camels, more than forty thousand goats, four thousand uqiyyah of silver. He did not distribute them. He waited more than ten nights. The thought was, if anyone of Hawazin came repenting, he would return their wealth. No one came. Then the distribution began.{{2}}
blocks.2: The first to be called were the chiefs of Makkah, who had only just come into Islam. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb (RA), Safwan ibn Umayyah, ‘Uyaynah ibn Hisn and Aqra‘ ibn Habis, each received a hundred camels. ‘Abbas ibn Mirdas received less than that. He said in verse,
blocks.4: Will you divide the plunder of me and of my companions between ‘Uyaynah and al-Aqra‘?{{1}}
blocks.5: The Prophet {{1}} completed his hundred too. Now about Safwan. To Safwan the Prophet {{2}} gave a hundred, again a hundred, again a hundred, three hundred camels in all. Later Safwan (RA) used to say,
blocks.7: By Allah, what the Prophet {{1}} gave me, he gave at a time when he was the most disliked of people to me. He kept giving until he became the dearest of people to me.{{2}}
blocks.8: The one who is not gathering this wealth but giving it away, the reason for his giving he himself has stated,
blocks.10: I give to Quraysh to win their hearts, because they have only just come up out of Jahiliyyah.{{1}}
blocks.11: For one who has only just come up from shirk, the smallest way to pull him up by the hand is perhaps a gift. For a man whose house and honour have been broken, before the question, honour comes first. The man Safwan disliked most, by giving and giving, that very man became dearest to him. The bedouins, hoping for goods, crowded around the Prophet {{1}}. Pushing and pushing they took him to a thorn tree. His cloak caught in the tree’s thorns. He stood and said,
blocks.13: Give me my cloak. By Allah, if I had camels equal in number to these thorn trees, I would distribute all of them among you. Then you would find me neither stingy, nor a liar, nor a coward.{{1}}
blocks.14: Then he plucked a tuft of wool from his camel’s hump, held it in his hand and said, people, not even this bit of wool is mine. Then he said,
blocks.16: Of the fay’ that Allah has given you, my share is only the fifth; and that fifth too is returned among you.{{1}}
blocks.17: One who pays such a price when giving is this detached about his own share. The cloak caught in the thorn tree too he gives, but not even his bit of wool. For the one into whose hand wealth comes, the test is exactly here. For one to whom rank and wealth are places of service, he settles others’ shares before taking his own. The foot soldiers got four camels or forty goats; the horsemen got three times that. Zayd ibn Thabit (RA) gathered everyone and explained the accounts.
blocks.19: There was a gap in that distribution at Ji‘ranah. The chiefs of Makkah got a hundred camels each. The Ansar got nothing at all. The Ansar who had sheltered the Prophet {{1}} in the face of the swords of Makkah’s enemies, whose swords had flashed at Hunayn too. Some young men of the Ansar whispered among themselves, may Allah forgive the Prophet {{2}}, he is giving to the Quraysh, leaving us out, though their blood still drips from our swords. The word reached the ears of Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubadah (RA). He came and told the Prophet {{3}}. The Prophet {{4}} asked, what is your own view about this? Sa‘d said, I am only one of my people. The Prophet {{5}} said, gather your people in this place. In a leather tent only the Ansar were gathered. A few Muhajirun came, they were not allowed to enter. When all had gathered the Prophet {{6}} came and asked, what word has come to me from you? The elder jurists of the Ansar said, O Messenger of Allah, our leaders said nothing. But a few young ones have said such a thing. The Prophet {{7}}, praising Allah, said,
blocks.21: O people of the Ansar! What is this word of yours that has reached me? Did I not find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? You were divided, and Allah united you through me? You were needy, and Allah enriched you through me?{{1}}
blocks.22: Each time he asked a question, the Ansar said in reply, Allah and His Messenger are more gracious. Then he said, if you wish you can say this too: you came to us in a state when you were being called a liar, we affirmed you as truthful; you came helpless, we helped you; you had been driven out, we sheltered you; you were in need, we comforted you. By Allah, if you say this you will be telling the truth, and your word will be accepted as true.{{1}}
blocks.23: Then he explained the reason for his decision. Quraysh had only just come from Jahiliyyah and calamity. He had wanted to make up their loss, to win their hearts. Then he said,
blocks.25: Are you not satisfied that people go back with goats and camels, and you go back to your homes with the Prophet {{1}}? By Allah, what you are returning with is better than what they are returning with.{{2}}
blocks.28: If all the people go into one valley and the Ansar into another mountain pass, I would choose the pass of the Ansar.{{1}}
blocks.29: The Ansar began to weep. Weeping, their beards were soaked. They said, we are satisfied with the Messenger of Allah {{1}}. The Prophet {{2}} then said, O Allah, have mercy on the Ansar, on the children of the Ansar, and on the children of their children. The Prophet {{3}} left the gathering. The people went back, each to his own. This incident is arranged in five steps. First, hearts were broken, this news reached him; Sa‘d did not suppress the word. Second, he did not wait, thinking it would be fine as time passed; that very day he called them and gathered everyone. Third, only the Ansar, no outsider. In a private meeting the complainers do not have to be ashamed. The fourth step is harder still. He himself composed, on the Ansar’s behalf, the very language of the complaint, and said, if you say this you will be telling the truth. The one against whom the complaint is, he himself said the strongest word of the complainers. Where is this courtesy today? The fifth step, not wealth, he gave himself. I am yours, my life is your life. He explained why that day he had given wealth to the new people of Makkah, and put into the Ansar’s hands what cannot be bought with wealth: himself. We often think, someone’s heart has been broken, it will be fine as time passes. What time can do is make the broken place set hard, joined wrongly. The decision is mine, taken with good intention. But how it felt to the one on whom the shadow of that decision has fallen, I will not know unless I ask.
blocks.31: In the meantime a delegation of fourteen from Hawazin arrived as Muslims. Their leader was Zuhayr ibn Surad. Among them was a milk-uncle of the Prophet {{1}}, Abu Burqan. They took the pledge and said, O Messenger of Allah, among those you have taken captive are our mothers, sisters, paternal aunts and maternal aunts. This is a great humiliation for us. They said in verse, be gracious to us, you are a man from whom hope can be held; have mercy on the women whose milk you once drank. Among these captives was the Prophet’s {{2}} milk-sister Shayma’ bint al-Harith (RA). She came to the Prophet {{3}} and gave her identity, the Prophet {{4}} spread out his cloak and seated her with honour, then graciously sent her back. That story will come in full in Dars 27.{{5}}
blocks.32: The Prophet {{1}} said to the delegation, the people you see with me, the dearest word to me is the true word. So say, which is dearer to you, children and women, or wealth?
blocks.34: The dearest word to me is the true word.{{1}}
blocks.35: They said, nothing is dearer to us than lineage and honour. The Prophet {{1}} said, after the Zuhr prayer you stand and say, we make the Messenger of Allah an intercessor with the believers, and the believers with the Messenger of Allah. They did so. The Prophet {{2}} said, what has fallen to my share and that of Banu ‘Abd al-Muttalib is given to you; from the others too I will ask for you. The Muhajirun and the Ansar at once stood up and said, everything of our share is for the Messenger of Allah. But Aqra‘ ibn Habis and ‘Uyaynah ibn Hisn, the two chiefs, said, we will not give our share. Nor ‘Abbas ibn Mirdas. Banu Sulaym said, everything of ours is for the Messenger of Allah. Then ‘Abbas ibn Mirdas said, you have struck my honour dead! The Prophet {{3}} said, they have come as Muslims. It was for them that I delayed the distribution. If any of you has a captive, if he gives gladly, good. And whoever wants to keep his share must return that too. In exchange, in the first victory that comes ahead, I will give six in place of one. All together the announcement was made. Everyone agreed to return the captives. In the end ‘Uyaynah too agreed.{{4}}
blocks.36: Where not everyone agreed, the Prophet {{1}} did not force. He said, I do not know which of you gives gladly and which does not. So go back. Your representatives will come and tell me.
blocks.38: We do not know who among you has consented and who has not. So go back, let your representatives convey your opinion to us.{{1}}
blocks.39: When wealth that people had won by fighting had to be returned, the Prophet {{1}} gave as much as he could from his own and asked the rest; but he did not put his hand over anyone’s mouth. Not silent consent, but confirmation through a representative. Where someone has a right, no decision without hearing everyone’s voice. The commander of Hawazin, Malik ibn ‘Awf, was hiding in the fortress of Ta’if. The Prophet {{2}} sent word, if he comes as a Muslim, he will get back his family and wealth, and a hundred camels besides. Malik came out secretly and accepted Islam. The very man who at Hunayn had raised the sword in front of the Muslims later wrote his name in history as a heroic commander of Islam.{{3}}
blocks.40: The Qur’an had told of that moment beforehand. Right after speaking of the punishment at Hunayn,
blocks.42: Then after that Allah grants repentance to whom He wills. Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.{{1}}
blocks.43: The one from whom we are being hurt today may tomorrow be our most trusted companion. For whom Allah will open the door of repentance, I do not know. My task is to keep my own door open.
blocks.44: A Complaint in the Name of Justice
blocks.45: At Ji‘ranah the silver was then being distributed. Silver in Bilal’s (RA) cloth; the Prophet {{1}} was taking handfuls from it and giving to people. From the crowd a man came and stood. He said, Muhammad, be just. The Prophet {{2}} said,
blocks.47: Woe to you! If I do not do justice, then who will do justice? If I do not do justice, then you have failed and lost.{{1}}
blocks.48: Hearing the word ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) said, O Messenger of Allah, let me go, I will strike off this hypocrite’s neck. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.50: Allah forbid! Let people not say that I kill my companions. This man and his companions will recite the Qur’an, it will not go below their throats. They will leave the religion as an arrow passes through the game.{{1}}
blocks.51: The man’s name was Dhu al-Khuwaysirah, of Banu Tamim. He had not come as an enemy of the Muslims. He had come thinking himself a man on the side of justice. But the Prophet’s {{1}} reckoning of justice did not seem right in his eyes. When saying it, on his lips was the appeal to justice, and inside, the audacity to put the Prophet {{2}} on trial. The Prophet {{3}} warned at once, next to the prayer of his companions you will think your own prayer small. But it will not cross their throats. Many years later a man with that mark was found in the battle of Nahrawan with ‘Ali (RA), and Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (RA) was a witness.{{4}}
blocks.52: Why did he not let Dhu al-Khuwaysirah be killed? ‘People will say, Muhammad kills his companions.’ Even when harsh words were spoken directly against himself, his concern was not about his own dignity; it was about people’s trust in Islam. And at the same time he also told the sign of a future fitnah: those whose prayer and fasting will shame you, they will recite the Qur’an, yet leave the religion. From seeing prayer and Qur’an, someone’s being on the truth is not proved. And again, seeing sarcasm in the name of justice, someone’s intention cannot be caught either. The measure is only one: how he stands before the Messenger. A complaint in which there is no humility has little justice, much arrogance.

blocks.1: At Ji‘ranah itself the Prophet {{1}} put on ihram. Coming to Makkah he performed ‘umrah. Anas (RA) said,
blocks.3: The Prophet {{1}} performed four ‘umrahs, all in Dhu al-Qa‘dah; the ‘umrah of Hudaybiyah, the ‘umrah of the next year, the ‘umrah from Ji‘ranah where he had distributed the spoils of Hunayn, and the ‘umrah with Hajj.{{2}}
blocks.4: After completing it the Prophet {{1}} appointed ‘Attab ibn Usayd (RA) as governor of Makkah. Then he set out toward Madinah. On the twenty-fourth of Dhu al-Qa‘dah of the eighth year of Hijrah, he entered that long-familiar Madinah.{{2}}
blocks.5: The city that for twenty years had struck him, that city came into his hand, and he handed its charge to someone like ‘Attab, who was still new in Islam. But how the administration of Makkah should be, the principles of it the Prophet {{1}} told with his own mouth. If you ask for a post, not the post. Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari (RA) says, I and two of my people went to the Prophet {{2}}. One of them said, make us governors. The other said the same. The Prophet {{3}} said,
blocks.7: By Allah, we do not appoint to this work anyone who has asked for it, or who has coveted it.{{1}}
blocks.8: Abu Musa himself had not asked for that work, so he was the one sent to Yemen. He gave Mu‘adh ibn Jabal as his companion, and told them,
blocks.10: Make things easy, do not make them hard. Give good news, do not drive people away. Work in agreement, do not differ.{{1}}
blocks.11: One to whom a post is service does not run after posts. One to whom a post is power asks for posts the most. And the one who gets a post must remember first of all: make it easy, do not drive away, work in harmony. A man from Egypt came to ‘A’ishah (RA). ‘A’ishah asked, how has your ruler behaved with you? The man said, no complaint. If someone’s camel died he gave a camel, if a slave died a slave, if expenses were needed he gave expenses. ‘A’ishah (RA) then said, then listen, I heard the Messenger of Allah {{1}} say in this very house of mine,
blocks.13: O Allah, whoever is given charge of any matter of my ummah and is harsh with them, be harsh with him. And whoever is given charge of any matter of my ummah and is gentle with them, be gentle with him.{{1}}
blocks.14: And Ma‘qil ibn Yasar (RA), on his deathbed, said to the governor ‘Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad, if I had known I would live, I would not say this today. I heard the Messenger of Allah {{1}} say,
blocks.16: A servant to whom Allah gives charge of a people, who dies on the day he dies while cheating his subjects, Allah will forbid Paradise to him.{{1}}
blocks.17: The Qur’an has spoken of this very trust in this way,
blocks.19: (O Muslims!) Surely Allah commands you to deliver trusts to their rightful owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Be sure that what Allah counsels you is most excellent. Surely Allah hears everything, sees everything.{{1}}
blocks.20: A trust is not just money. A post is a trust, a decision is a trust, a person’s reliance is a trust. A sign of keeping a trust: at the time of delivering it to the rightful one, recognising him, remembering, not cheating someone and keeping it for oneself.
blocks.22: The Prophet {{1}} was at once commander, giver and judge. A few rules of sitting in the seat of judgement he told with his own mouth. Umm Salamah (RA) says, the Prophet {{2}} said,
blocks.24: You bring disputes to me. Perhaps some of you can arrange your argument better than another. If, hearing his words, I give him something of his brother’s right, then I have cut for him a piece of Hell; let him not take it.{{1}}
blocks.25: This is the word of a judge who is himself a prophet, upon whom revelation descends. Yet he admitted, I am a human; if someone states his argument beautifully I may give a ruling on his word. But even if I rule, the one who knows the right is not his, if he takes it he has taken a piece of fire. A judge’s ruling does not make the haram halal for anyone. Even if it is written on the court’s paper. Another rule, which Abu Bakrah (RA) wrote to his son who was in Sijistan. He had heard the Prophet {{1}} say,
blocks.27: Let no judge decide between two while he is angry.{{1}}
blocks.28: When angry a person forgets justice. A judge is only human; anger rises in him. So at the time of anger there is no seat for him. Today, those of us who take decisions about anyone, at home, in the office, in the madrasah, when there is anger let us pause for a while. A ruling given in anger never comes in the name of justice; it comes in the name of revenge.
blocks.29: The Market and the Bayt al-Mal
blocks.30: In today’s language, the Prophet {{1}} was then running a state. What the rules were for that state’s market, treasury and wealth, a few pictures are found in sahih narrations. The market. The Prophet {{2}} himself would go out to look at the market. One day, passing by a heap of foodgrain, he put in his hand and found it wet. He asked the owner, what is this? He said, it got wet in the rain, O Messenger of Allah. He said, why did you not put the wet part on top, so that people could see? Then he said,
blocks.32: Whoever cheats is not of me.{{1}}
blocks.33: In our market today dry goods are arranged on top and wet goods below. With the Prophet {{1}}, for this cheating not just a fine but a declaration: he is not of me. There is another matter he also told, which pulls at the very root of the market,
blocks.35: The Prophet {{1}} cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who gives riba, its writer and its two witnesses. He said, they are all the same.{{2}}
blocks.36: Those who write down the accounts of riba, they too. Those who are witnesses, they too. Four hands in one transaction. In the business of riba no one can think himself outside. The Bayt al-Mal. The wealth that comes into hand without war is called fay’. The rules for distributing it Allah Himself has fixed. The Qur’an says it in this way,
blocks.38: The wealth that Allah has granted His Messenger as ‘fay’’ from the people of other towns belongs to Allah, His Messenger, (the Messenger’s) relatives, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarers, so that it does not circulate only among the wealthy among you. Take what the Messenger gives you, and refrain from what he forbids you, and fear Allah. Surely Allah is severe in punishment.{{1}}
blocks.39: So that the wealth does not circulate only among the wealthy; this condition is the root formula of a state’s economy. A system in which wealth goes and accumulates in one place, in the Qur’an’s language that system is itself on the road to breakdown. And the one who was the guardian of that wealth, what was his own reckoning? ‘Uqbah ibn al-Harith (RA) says, one day after ‘Asr the Prophet {{1}} gave the salam and rose quickly, stepped over people’s necks and went to his wife’s room. The people were alarmed. Coming out he said,
blocks.41: In my house some pieces of gold of the sadaqah were lying. I remembered. I did not want it to hold me back, so I ordered its distribution.{{1}}
blocks.42: A little gold of the sadaqah had remained in the house, and his restlessness over it. Today we leave office files, an organisation’s funds, a mosque’s donations lying in the house or the car; to him even one piece of gold was heavy to keep a night in the house. Waqf. Instead of hoarding wealth, the way of turning it into lasting good too the Prophet {{1}} showed. ‘Umar (RA) got a piece of land at Khaybar, than which he had never got more precious wealth. He asked the Prophet {{2}}, what shall I do? The Prophet {{3}} said,
blocks.44: If you wish, hold its principal and give its fruit as sadaqah.{{1}}
blocks.45: ‘Umar (RA) did just that. The land would not be sold, would not be given away, would not go by inheritance. Its fruit would go for the poor, relatives, freeing slaves, the way of Allah, wayfarers and guests. Whoever is in charge of looking after it may eat in a just manner, but may not accumulate wealth. The wealth I love most, by giving that to someone I have truly given. And I gave it in such a way that it will be of use forever. Waqf means this thought: even if I am gone, the thing I love will keep working for people.
blocks.47: About those who live under a covenant in a Muslim state, the Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.49: Whoever kills a mu‘ahad will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though the fragrance of Paradise can be smelled from a distance of forty years.{{1}}
blocks.50: To kill a non-Muslim citizen means being deprived even of the fragrance of Paradise. Yet that fragrance can be smelled from a distance of forty years. In this hadith the safety of the state’s weakest citizen is not just law but a condition of faith. And the right of the worker. Allah Himself has declared that He will be the plaintiff against three,
blocks.52: Allah says, on the Day of Resurrection I am the plaintiff against three: one who gave a promise in My name and then broke it; one who sold a free person and ate his price; and one who hired a labourer and extracted the full work from him, yet did not give his wages.{{1}}
blocks.53: Withholding wages is here in the same row as breaking a contract and selling people to eat their price. In today’s terms, not paying salary on time, cheating by working overtime, taking money in the name of giving a job, before these Allah Himself will stand on the Day of Resurrection. And the subordinate people, domestic workers, employees, slaves. Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA) once abused someone by taunting him about his mother. The Prophet {{1}} said, you are a man in whom there is Jahiliyyah. Then he said,
blocks.55: Your brothers are your subordinates. Allah has placed them under your hands. Whoever has his brother under his hand, let him feed him what he himself eats; clothe him in what he himself wears. And do not burden them with work that is beyond them. If you must burden them, help them.{{1}}
blocks.56: Abu Dharr dressed that slave like himself. People saw him at Rabadhah, one pair of clothes on his own body, one pair on the slave’s body too. By one word of the Prophet {{1}} a Companion changed the rule of his own house. Non-Muslim citizen, worker, subordinate. In the Prophet’s {{2}} state the rights of each of these are in the clear declarations of the Qur’an and hadith. Cheating in the market is forbidden; wealth shall circulate among all; if you ask for a post, not the post. The one who, seeing the hearts of the Ansar break, called them aside and explained, he too stands beside a heap of grain in the market. The same man. The heart that thinks about the Ansar’s hearts, that very heart thinks about a poor labourer’s wages too.
blocks.57: A Few More Commonly Circulated Narrations
blocks.58: About a few matters of this dars there are some more narrations that people tell or that are found in books. They too have been kept here. The chain and grade of each is given in the footnote. First, a narration on the rights of non-Muslims under a covenant. The sons of a group of Companions narrate from their fathers that the Messenger of Allah {{1}} said,
blocks.60: Beware! Whoever wrongs a non-Muslim under a covenant, reduces his right, burdens him beyond his capacity, or takes something from him without his satisfaction, I will be the plaintiff against him on the Day of Resurrection.{{1}}
blocks.61: Protecting those under covenant from all these forms of wrong is the Prophet’s {{1}} command. A narration on the worker’s wages is very commonly circulated, which is basically said in these words,
blocks.62: Give the labourer his wages before his sweat dries.{{1}}
blocks.63: Paying the worker’s right quickly, that is the idea here. There is a narration from Ibn Mas‘ud (RA) on the number of Companions at Hunayn. He says,
blocks.64: On the day of Hunayn we were with the Messenger of Allah {{1}}. The people drew back from him. And with him remained eighty Muhajirun and Ansar. We went back almost eighty paces, but we did not turn our backs.{{2}}
blocks.65: Whatever the number of those who were with the Prophet {{1}}, they did not turn their backs. There is a narration of Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA) on the Prophet’s {{2}} du‘a for Thaqif beneath the fortress of Ta’if. The Companions said,
blocks.66: O Messenger of Allah, the arrows of Thaqif have burned us, curse them. He said, O Allah, guide Thaqif.{{1}}
blocks.67: Even for the enemy a prayer of guidance, this was his way. Finally a Sirah-based story, which is now found in many books. About Abu Bakrah Nufay‘ ibn al-Harith (RA),
blocks.68: When the Messenger of Allah {{1}} besieged the fortress of Ta’if, I came down from the fortress with the help of a pulley and came to the Messenger of Allah {{2}}. He asked, how did you come down? I said, by a pulley. He said, you are Abu Bakrah (the pulley-man).{{3}}
blocks.69: A slave came down from the fortress wall and came over to the side of Islam, and his very name became ‘Abu Bakrah’.
blocks.71: From Hunayn to Ji‘ranah, then Madinah, a few pictures of these few weeks stay in the mind. The new Muslims’ wish on seeing the jujube tree of Dhat Anwat, and the Prophet’s {{1}} correcting it at once. In the army of twelve thousand the words ‘today we will not lose’, and the rain of arrows of one dawn. A man on a white mule, I am the Prophet, no lie. People returning at ‘Abbas’s single call. Abu ‘Amir’s last words, tell the Prophet {{2}} to seek forgiveness for me. ‘We are returning’ for the Companions who stumbled beneath the fortress of Ta’if. On the lips not a curse but a prayer of guidance. Safwan in the tent at Ji‘ranah, whose dislike turned to love. The cloak caught on the thorn tree and a tuft of wool in the fist. The weeping of the Ansar, their beards wet. The delegation of Hawazin, the cloak spread for the milk-sister, Malik ibn ‘Awf’s return. Dhu al-Khuwaysirah’s ‘be just’. The charge of Makkah, the trust, the seat of judgement, the market, the Bayt al-Mal, the worker’s wages. We take decisions. In our own house, shop, office, madrasah, organisation. The reckoning of the decision is clear to us. But whose heart broke that day, we do not see. So take away one deed from today’s dars.
blocks.73: The Ansar had taken offence. The Prophet {{1}} did not brush it off, he called them aside and explained, and they wept. Today I will ask myself a question: by which of my decisions has someone’s heart been broken, and did I notice it, or did I assume it will be fine as time passes? Today the one whose heart my decision broke I will call aside and explain to, and I will listen to what they say too; I will not give up this habit from today.
